description: Every Mars map shows the terrain. We map the body. LAND & STAND fuses NASA post-flight physiology, spacesuit metabolic data and real Gale crater topography into a probabilistic map of where each astronaut can walk on sol 1. Team: 3 software developers (one ex-cybersecurity consultant), a systems engineer, a nurse, and a psychologist and future MD lecturing in biostatistics; two MBAs. Seeking human factors, data viz, design, video and storytelling talent.
summary: Every Mars map describes the terrain. LAND & STAND adds the missing layer: the astronaut’s body. After six months in microgravity, the first crews will land with reduced aerobic capacity and impaired balance, and up to 22 minutes away from Earth by radio. We built an interactive map of the real terrain at the base of Mount Sharp, Gale crater, that shows sol by sol the probability that a specific crew member, or a pair, can walk to a real Curiosity science site and return within the suit’s time and energy budget. The model combines NASA data on post-flight physiology and spacesuit walking costs with the USGS elevation model of Gale, and propagates uncertainty with Monte Carlo simulation. Climbing matters more than distance: Rock Hall, on Vera Rubin Ridge, is 29% reachable on sol 1, against 78% for the same distance on flat ground. The tool also shows where to land, which design choices matter most and what to measure first. Instead of “safe zones”, we show what is reachable, for whom, how likely, and under which explicit assumptions.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

LAND & STAND is an interactive map and route forecaster for the first walks on Mars. For a real 3.5 × 3.5 km area at the base of Mount Sharp, Gale crater, it shows, before each EVA and sol by sol, the probability that a specific astronaut, a pair or a group can walk from the habitat to any point, do a 30-minute task and return within the suit’s time and energy budget. The crew chooses who goes out (eight forecast crew profiles), the sol (1 to 30) and the walking pace, and sees the probability for every 32 m cell, for six mission destinations proposed by the team and for six real Curiosity sites, such as Rock Hall on Vera Rubin Ridge and Mary Anning in Glen Torridon, with the rover’s photographs and 360° panoramas. Tapping any point draws the minimum-energy route out and back, with its length, climb and steepest slope. The crew can also add its own destinations.

The model has four building blocks:

  1. Post-landing recovery of aerobic capacity and balance, calibrated with Bayesian inference on NASA data from ISS crews.
  2. The metabolic cost of walking in a pressurized suit in simulated Martian gravity, adjusted for slope. Descents are never faster than flat walking, to account for fall risk with impaired balance.
  3. Minimum-energy round-trip routes (Dijkstra) on the USGS elevation model of Gale, built from HiRISE, CTX and HRSC data.
  4. A Monte Carlo simulation with 300 scenarios that separates differences between astronauts from what we still do not know. In pair and group modes, everyone must succeed in the same scenario.

Everything runs in the browser, split across up to six Web Workers; a forecast for a group of three takes under a second. The plan is computed before departure and nothing is recomputed during the walk. The tool opens with a short scroll-driven presentation, works in English and Spanish, and adapts to a habitat screen, a tablet or a phone.

Benefits:

  • Plans EVAs around the real crew, not an average astronaut: on sol 1, Rock Hall ranges from 2% for the most deconditioned profile to 91% for the fittest.
  • Turns the forecast into a schedule: Rock Hall becomes likely on sol 1 for three profiles, on sol 14 for the reference astronaut, and not within 30 sols for two profiles.
  • Pairs and groups: in 97% of cases the team’s probability equals that of its weakest member, so the tool names who limits the group.
  • Shows which choices matter most. Five points of walking pace are worth a month of recovery. With Apollo’s 4-hour life-support budget, Rock Hall drops from 29% to 6% on sol 1.
  • Identifies what to measure first: planning with each crew member’s measured fitness raises the expected value of the first walk by 21–44%, and the suit’s walking-cost curve is the key missing data.
  • Suggests where to land: a site on Vera Rubin Ridge raises the expected number of reachable sites on sol 1 from 2.6 to 4.3 of 6.

Intended impact:

  • Support Earth-independent decision-making for crews that are up to 22 minutes away from Earth by radio.
  • Give a clear research priority: suited walking cost in partial gravity, for example in NASA’s ARGOS facility.
  • The same approach applies to Artemis on the Moon and, on Earth, to mountain rescue, polar stations and rehabilitation of patients after long hospital stays.
  • Next steps: a season and departure-time selector with Curiosity weather data, an estimated radiation dose per EVA from Curiosity’s RAD instrument, a checkpoint schedule, and graded alarms fixed in the plan before departure.

Tools:

  • Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript; Three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D globe and terrain; d3 for map zoom, scales and contours; Tailwind CSS.
  • Web Workers for parallel Monte Carlo computation in the browser.
  • Vitest (92 automated tests, covering every model layer against the algorithm specification), ESLint, and Git and GitHub for version control: github.com/raaulalonso/LandAndStand
  • Python (rasterio, NumPy, Pillow) for the scripts that rebuild the terrain grid and the imagery from the official USGS files.
  • Data: USGS MSL Gale Merged DEM (1 m), HiRISE colour mosaic, CTX mosaic, Viking MDIM 2.1 and MOLA for the globe, NASA/JPL Curiosity waypoints and NASA Photojournal images.
  • We used AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) under the team’s direction, as declared below.

Creativity:

Most Mars maps describe the terrain; ours maps human capability onto it. We replace “safe zones” with probabilities under explicit assumptions, add time after landing as a dimension of the map, and compute where to land by running the route search backwards from each target.

Factors we considered:

  • Scientific honesty: every probability is conditional on stated assumptions, and we never label terrain “safe”.
  • Uncertainty quantification, Sobol sensitivity analysis, value of information, and robustness tests (16 m resolution, habitat position, grid geometry, loose sand).
  • A NASA-STD-7009B credibility self-assessment: fit for a demonstration, not yet for operations; validation needs suited walking data at 0.38 g.
  • Ethics and privacy in using individual health data for EVA decisions.
  • Human-in-the-loop design: the tool advises; the crew, the flight surgeon and mission control decide.
